newsitem.title: USA: Emerging debt dips on renewed U.S. rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Emerging debt dips on renewed U.S. rate fears.

text.p: Most emerging markets debt suffered from a more-negative outlook on U.S. interest rates, slackening for the first time in several days, market experts said.

"Trading accounts overall were better sellers for the day, and that was mostly bridged on a view of U.S. interest rates and the fact that (spreads) tightened too much in the last week," one trader said.
Losses hit the various Latin issues fairly evenly, while Eastern Europe fared better.
Brazil "C" bonds fell two points to 76-5/8 bid. With state mining concern Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) successfully auctioned, traders said, Brazil had gotten past the good news.
"Buy the rumor, sell the fact -- you had that sort of mentality happening," another trader said.
Argentina FRBs were off 7/8 at 92-1/8 bid, and Mexico pars were off 1-1/2 at 72-7/8 bid.
Eastern Europe found some encouragement in announcements of a Brady buyback in Poland and a planned signing date for a debt rescheduling agreement in Russia, experts said.
Poland's finance ministry said it had bought $1.69 billion of Bradys, primarily discount paper.
The operation probably was carried out over several months to prevent market shocks, analysts said. A desire to improve Poland's credit rating may have prompted the effort, they said.
Poland discount bonds were up 1/4 at 97-3/4 bid, and RSTAs were up 1/2 at 61-3/8.

Russia's announcement that it plans to sign a debt rescheduling agreement with the London Club by June 30 helped to support the country's Vnesh loan prices as other emerging markets issues faltered, traders and analysts said.
Dollar-denominated Vnesh loans were off 1/8 at 83-3/8 bid, while mark- and Swiss franc-denominated Vnesh were unchanged.
U.S. analysts agreed the statement was good news, but some questioned whether it revealed any specific timetable for completing the rescheduling.
"I've been following the saga of this restructuring agreement for a long time, and that was music to my ears," said Peter Allen, head of emerging markets research at Bank of Boston.
The stumbling block for Russia, however, remains the process of reconciling the required $20 billion, Allen said.
He said Wednesday's statement could be interpreted two ways: Russia is either confident it can reconcile the required amount by June 30, or it is merely hopeful.
